title: Optimal Attention Temperature Improves the Robustness of In-Context Learning under Distribution Shift in High Dimensions
claim: Temperature reshapes the output distribution of softmax and of its tractable approximation in the same way, which justifies analyzing the approximation.
layout: 4 histogram panels, left-to-right, shared τ color legend with dashed 1/ℓ reference line
description: A single row of four histogram panels. The leftmost panel, 'input', shows a roughly uniform probability density with a sharp spike at 1.0, drawn in dark navy. The other three panels are titled 'softmax', 'approximate softmax' (with a hat over the word) and 'linear (with τ scaling)'. Each uses a log-scale y-axis from 10^-1 to 10^6 and overlays semi-transparent histograms for τ = 0.3 (blue), 1.0 (red) and 3 (green). A vertical dashed black line marks 1/ℓ in each panel. In the softmax panel, small τ spreads the values widely and large τ concentrates them near 1/ℓ. The approximate-softmax panel shows nearly the same pattern, with flatter bars. The linear panel shows the same ranges shifted, and its distributions start at 0 and do not center on 1/ℓ. The eye goes first to the colored overlapping blocks around the dashed line.
caption: Comparison of temperature effects in softmax, approximate softmax, and linear (with temperature scaling) cases. We consider an input vector $\vx \in \R^l$ whose histogram is illustrated on the left-most plot. Rest of the plots illustrates histograms of the elements of $softmax(\vx / \tau)$, approximation $\widehat{softmax}(\vx /\tau)$ derived in Appendix [ref] and $\vx/(l \tau)$ from left to right, respectively.
abstract: Pretrained Transformers can perform in-context learning (ICL) from a few demonstrations, but this ability can fail sharply when the test distribution differs from pretraining, a common deployment setting. We study attention temperature as a simple inference-time control for improving ICL robustness under such shifts. In a high-dimensional linear-regression framework, we analyze a Transformer with "approximate softmax" attention, which preserves softmax's normalization and temperature-dependent selectivity while remaining tractable. We derive a closed-form expression for the ICL generalization error under distribution shift, and show that it is minimized by an explicit optimal attention temperature. This characterization yields interpretable guidance by linking the best temperature to moments of the pre-softmax attention scores, and predicts when temperature adjustment can recover near Bayes-optimal performance. We validate the theory with extensive simulations, and further demonstrate gains on pretrained LLMs (GPT-2 and Llama2-7B) on question-answering benchmarks under distribution shift induced by noisy in-context demonstrations. Overall, attention temperature emerges as a principled, lightweight knob for improving the robustness of ICL in pretrained Transformers.
